planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring in deep, well-drained soil and support the long canes on a trellis; Meeker is a floricane type that fruits on second-year wood.

directions: Plant dormant bare-root canes in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and train the canes to a two-wire trellis, since the long, productive canes bend heavily under a full crop. Meeker is the classic Pacific Northwest commercial red raspberry, bred at Washington State University and long the dominant processing variety in Washington and Oregon, valued for its consistently large, firm, bright red conic berries with excellent flavor for both fresh eating and freezing. It fruits on floricanes, so remove spent canes to the ground after harvest each year and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest shoots. It performs best where summers are mild and winters are not severely cold, and can be prone to root rot in poorly drained soils.
sources: Washington State University Extension — Small Fruit Production
Oregon State University Extension — Raspberry Cultivars
Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; Killarney was bred for extreme cold hardiness and needs no special winter protection in most northern gardens.

directions: Plant dormant bare-root canes in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing rows to allow good air movement through the thicket. Killarney was released by the University of Manitoba specifically for prairie and northern climates and remains one of the most cold-hardy red raspberry cultivars available, reliably surviving winters that would damage many modern varieties. It bears a single summer crop of medium-sized, bright red, firmly textured berries with classic sweet-tart raspberry flavor on floricanes, so spent canes should be cut to the ground after harvest. Its toughness makes it a dependable choice for short-season gardens where more tender cultivars struggle.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing Raspberries
Manitoba Agriculture
Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring; Autumn Bliss fruits on current-season primocanes, so all canes can be mown to the ground each winter for simplified maintenance.

directions: Plant dormant canes in full sun in fertile, moisture-retentive soil, and cut all canes to the ground in late winter since fruit forms on the current season's growth. Bred at East Malling Research in England, Autumn Bliss was one of the first widely planted primocane (fall-bearing) raspberry cultivars and remains valued for ripening its crop earlier in the season than most other fall types, which is a real advantage in shorter-season gardens. The medium-to-large, dark red, conical berries have good flavor and hold reasonably well after picking, and the compact, sturdy canes often need little or no trellising. It can be more susceptible to certain cane diseases than newer primocane releases, so good air circulation and sanitation help keep it productive.
sources: East Malling Research variety notes
Royal Horticultural Society
Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring; Polka fruits on current-season primocanes and can be mown to the ground each winter or left partially unpruned for an added early summer crop.

directions: Plant dormant canes in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and mow all canes to the ground in late winter for the simplest management, since Polka is a primocane type that fruits reliably on first-year wood. Bred in Poland at the Brzezna research institute, Polka is a heavy-yielding fall raspberry known for large, firm, glossy conical berries with a pleasant sweet-tart flavor and good shelf life, making it popular with market growers as well as home gardeners. It ripens over a long fall window and holds up well to light rain without excessive fruit softening. Good air circulation and consistent moisture during fruiting help maximize berry size and reduce disease pressure.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide
Michigan State University Extension — Raspberry Production
Research Institute of Horticulture, Poland (Brzezna) variety notes

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring on a trellis in well-drained soil; Cascade Delight was bred for improved root rot resistance and can tolerate heavier soils better than older raspberry cultivars.

directions: Plant dormant bare-root canes in full sun in fertile soil and support the vigorous canes on a trellis, removing spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year. Released by Washington State University as an improvement on older Pacific Northwest cultivars like Meeker, Cascade Delight was specifically bred for resistance to Phytophthora root rot, a major limitation in wetter or heavier soils, while still producing large, firm, bright red conic berries with excellent flavor. It ripens slightly later than Meeker, extending the summer harvest window, and its firmer fruit holds up well for both fresh eating and shipping. Its improved disease resistance makes it a more forgiving choice than many older varieties for gardeners with imperfectly drained soil.
sources: Washington State University Extension — Small Fruit Production
Oregon State University Extension — Raspberry Cultivars
Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Boreal Beauty is self-infertile and needs a compatible University of Saskatchewan pollinizer, such as Boreal Blizzard, planted nearby for good fruit set.

directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, since Boreal Beauty needs cross-pollination from another haskap cultivar to crop well. Released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program as part of its 'Boreal' series, Boreal Beauty ripens later than the earliest haskap introductions and produces firm, elongated, deep-blue berries bred to hold well on the bush without dropping, making it well suited to mechanical or delayed hand harvest. Like other haskaps, it is exceptionally cold-hardy and thrives in short, cool-summer growing seasons, but it is not well adapted to hot, humid climates. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood for the first several years, then shift to renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep the bush productive.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Fruit Program — Haskap Cultivar Release Notes
Oregon State University Extension — Haskap/Honeyberry Production
Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Honeyberry Cultivar Trials

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Boreal Blizzard is self-infertile and is often planted specifically as a compatible pollinizer for other University of Saskatchewan haskap cultivars such as Boreal Beauty.

directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, as Boreal Blizzard will not set a meaningful crop without a compatible pollinizer nearby. Part of the University of Saskatchewan's 'Boreal' haskap series, Boreal Blizzard produces a heavy crop of good-flavored blue berries and blooms at a time that makes it an effective pollen source for several other Saskatchewan-bred cultivars, so it is commonly planted in pairs specifically to boost yields in a mixed haskap planting. The upright, vigorous shrub is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating deep winter cold typical of the Canadian prairies, but struggles in hot, humid summer regions. Limit pruning to removing dead or crossing wood while the bush is young, then begin renewal pruning of older canes once the planting is established.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Fruit Program — Haskap Cultivar Release Notes
Oregon State University Extension — Haskap/Honeyberry Production
Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Honeyberry Cultivar Trials

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes from autumn through early spring, burying the crown slightly deeper than it grew in the nursery to encourage strong new shoots from the base.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, setting the crown a couple of inches deeper than it sat in the pot to promote vigorous basal shoots. Bred in Scotland, Ben Connan is a compact black currant selection prized for combining a smaller, more garden-friendly bush size with very heavy yields of large, richly flavored berries, making it a popular choice where space is limited. It ripens earlier than many other black currant cultivars, giving a head start on the harvest season, and its dense, tidy growth habit needs less room between plants than older, larger currant varieties. Prune in the dormant season by removing about a quarter to a third of the oldest wood each year, since the best fruit forms on one- and two-year-old stems.
sources: James Hutton Institute — Soft Fruit Breeding
Royal Horticultural Society
Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes from autumn to early spring in cool-summer climates; gooseberries perform poorly where summers are hot and humid and appreciate afternoon shade in warmer regions.

directions: Plant dormant, thorny bushes in fertile, well-drained soil in a spot with cool root conditions, mulching to conserve moisture and prune to an open framework to make harvest through the spines easier. Careless is a traditional English culinary gooseberry long grown for its heavy, reliable crops of large, pale green, thin-skinned berries that are quite tart when picked early for cooking but sweeten as they ripen toward translucent pale yellow-green, making it equally suited to pies, fools, and preserves or later fresh eating. The vigorous, somewhat spreading bush is one of the most widely planted gooseberry cultivars in British gardens and allotments. Prune in the dormant season to an open, airy shape to improve light penetration and reduce mildew pressure on the ripening fruit.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society
University of Minnesota Extension
Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes from autumn to early spring; Whinham's Industry is notably tolerant of poor, heavy soils and partial shade compared with most other gooseberry cultivars.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, in full sun or light shade, and prune to an open vase shape each winter to ease harvesting among the thorny stems. A very old English cultivar dating to the mid-1800s, Whinham's Industry remains popular for its notable tolerance of poor, heavy, or shaded conditions where many other gooseberries struggle, along with strong resistance to American gooseberry mildew. Its medium-to-large, hairy-skinned berries ripen from green to a deep dusky red with a rich, sweet-tart flavor good for both dessert use and cooking. The vigorous, spreading habit and dependable heavy cropping have kept it a garden favorite for over a century.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society
University of Minnesota Extension
Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide
